description: Our team is Shruthi Subramaniam and Ishita Karkhanis, high school sophomores. For the Nasa Space Apps Challenge, we will be building an AI-powered dashboard that uses NASA’s microgravity combustion data to predict how fire behaves in space and help keep astronauts safe. We are two passionate high school girls ready to take on our challenge statement.
summary:
Our team, Space Debros, created an interactive dashboard called Flame in Freefall. We wanted to answer one question: what does NASA’s space fire research actually mean for astronauts going to the Moon and Mars?

Fire in space is odd. With no gravity, flames turn into slow blue balls, and some keep burning after they seem to have gone out. NASA has studied this for decades, but the findings are spread across dozens of research papers. Nobody has time to dig through all of that, so we did it for you.

We pulled 19 key findings from NASA’s FLEX, BASS and Saffire experiments. Then we ranked them by how dangerous they are, whether Earth tests would miss them, and how much they matter for Moon and Mars missions. Users can change the rankings, read mission briefings, or ask questions to a built-in AI assistant.

The part we’re proudest of is Habitat Check. You set the air inside a future habitat, and it shows which findings apply. That’s how we noticed something big: in air close to what NASA plans for Moon and Mars bases, turning off the fans didn’t quickly put out a fire, and NASA hasn’t tested that exact air at full scale yet.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Flame in Freefall is a website with seven tabs, and each one does a different job:

- Overview explains why fire acts weird without gravity and walks through 30 years of NASA fire research, from Space Shuttle tests to the Saffire fires set inside empty Cygnus cargo ships.

- Data has three charts: the lowest oxygen level that still let things burn, how airflow speeds up flames, and how planned habitat air compares to the Space Station. There's also a table of all 19 findings with their test conditions and sources, plus a list of things NASA hasn't tested yet.

- Rankings scores every finding from 1 to 5 on danger, whether Earth tests would miss it, and Moon/Mars relevance. You move the sliders to decide what matters most and the list re-sorts.

- Habitat Check lets you set the cabin pressure, oxygen level and airflow for a future base. It plots your air against every condition NASA has actually tested, tells you how close the nearest test is, and flags which findings apply.

- Missions gives a short fire safety briefing for a space station, a Moon base and a Mars mission.

- Ask answers questions using only our 19 findings and cites which ones it used.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Someone planning a mission or designing a habitat can get the big picture in a few minutes instead of reading dozens of papers. Every number links back to its NASA source, so nothing has to be taken on trust. We also want it to point researchers toward what still needs testing. The biggest example: NASA plans habitat air at 52.7-58.6 kPa and 30-34% oxygen, but the closest large space fire test (Saffire V) only reached about 71 kPa and 26%. Even then, turning off the fans didn't quickly stop the fire, and that's the main move astronauts use on the ISS.

TOOLS WE USED

HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the site, Chart.js for the charts, and GitHub Pages for hosting. We used Claude as an AI assistant to help summarize the research, suggest scores, and write and debug code. It also powers the Ask feature.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Most data dashboards just show numbers. Ours lets you rank findings by what you care about, and Habitat Check works more like a design tool: you build a habitat's air and it tells you what the evidence says. We also put the gaps front and center instead of hiding them, because what NASA hasn't tested matters as much as what it has.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

- Accuracy: we only used published NASA results and linked every source.

- Honesty: the scores are our own judgment, and we say so. Experiments used different setups, so we flag when numbers can't be directly compared.

- Who's reading: we wrote for someone with no science background, so there's no jargon without an explanation.

- Access: it runs in any browser with no login, and the Ask tab still works without AI by searching the findings directly.
